title: Wisdom and Strength Belong to God
summary: Job answers his friends with sarcasm: surely wisdom will die with them. He knows everything they know, yet he has become a laughingstock while robbers live securely. The animals and the earth themselves know that the LORD's hand is behind everything, and Job describes a God of such wisdom and power that he overturns counselors, judges, kings, priests, and whole nations.
story: Zophar has just told Job that God is punishing him less than he deserves and has urged him to repent (chapter 11). With that, all three friends have spoken once. Job's reply runs through chapters 12 to 14, his longest speech so far, and closes the first round of the debate. Chapter 12 answers the friends' claim to superior wisdom. Job agrees with them that God is wise and all-powerful; what he rejects is their conclusion that this power always rewards the good and punishes the wicked in ways anyone can see. Looking at the world as it actually is, Job sees God's power displayed in overturning, tearing down, and confusing the mighty, and this makes the neat moral order of the friends look naive.
historical:
The second half of the chapter (verses 17-25) reads like a survey of what happened to royal courts and nations in the ancient Near East. Kingdoms rose and fell in Job's world with startling speed. Assyria dominated the region for much of the eighth and seventh centuries BC and then collapsed within a few years of Nineveh's fall in 612 BC; Babylon rose in its place and itself fell to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC. Counselors, priests, and judges were carried off with their kings. Job's poem does not name any of these events, and it would fit many periods, but readers who knew such history would hear its truth.

The chapter also contains the only use of God's personal name, the LORD (YHWH, the covenant name revealed to Israel), in the poetic dialogue between Job and his friends (verse 9). Elsewhere in chapters 3 to 37 the speakers use general names like El, Eloah, and Shaddai, fitting their setting outside Israel. A few Hebrew manuscripts read God here instead, and the same line appears word for word in Isaiah 41:20, which may explain its presence.
cultural:
Being made a laughingstock (verse 4) was a serious harm in an honor culture. A man's standing in the community, his name at the city gate, and his voice among the elders were central to his life. For Job, who had been honored in public (chapter 29 will describe it), becoming a joke was a second loss after his wealth and health. Verse 5 names a common human reflex: those at ease look down on people in trouble, as though misfortune were a sign of weakness.

The picture of counselors and priests led away barefoot (verses 17 and 19) comes from the treatment of captives. Conquering armies stripped prisoners of their sandals and outer clothing and marched them into exile, a public humiliation Isaiah acted out when he walked barefoot as a sign of Egyptian captives led off by Assyria (Isaiah 20:2-4). Loosening the bonds of kings and binding a belt on them (verse 18) may picture a king's royal sash replaced with a captive's rope.
literary: The chapter falls into three parts. Verses 1-6 are personal: biting sarcasm (“Truly then you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die!”), a claim to equal knowledge, and a complaint about being mocked while the wicked prosper. Verses 7-12 appeal to the created world as a teacher, echoing the wisdom tradition's habit of learning from animals (compare Proverbs 6:6). Verses 13-25 are a long hymn to God's wisdom and power, but an unusual one. Where most hymns celebrate God raising the lowly, this one dwells on God humbling the high: the verbs are tearing down, imprisoning, withholding, overthrowing, and confusing. The final image, leaders groping in darkness and staggering like drunkards, turns the friends' confident talk of order upside down.

outline.t: Job's sarcasm: I know what you know
Ask the animals: the LORD's hand has done this
Wisdom and power belong to God
God overturns the mighty and the wise

doctrines.note: “The life of every living thing is in His hand, as well as the breath of all mankind” (verse 10). Job and his friends agree that God rules everything; they disagree about what that rule looks like from inside human history.
Verse 13 is one of the chapter's central claims: wisdom and strength belong to God. Human wisdom, even that of elders, counselors, and priests, is borrowed and can be taken away.

God's governance of history includes raising and bringing down nations (verse 23). Job's picture emphasizes the hardness of that governance, a side of providence that tidy accounts of reward and punishment tend to leave out.

words.note: Chokmah, wisdom. In the Old Testament it means skill in living well, practical and moral, grounded in the fear of God. It appears three times in this chapter: mockingly of the friends (verse 2), of the elderly (verse 12), and finally of God (verse 13), to whom it truly belongs.

YHWH, the personal name of Israel's God, usually printed as LORD in small capitals in English Bibles. Its lone appearance in the poetic dialogue at verse 9 is striking, since the speakers otherwise use more general divine names.

Tohu, formlessness or emptiness, the word used for the earth before creation in Genesis 1:2 (formless). In verse 24 God makes the earth's leaders wander in a trackless tohu, as if their world were returned to a state before order.
Sholal, barefoot or stripped, a word describing captives led away. It appears in verses 17 and 19 of counselors and priests, the wise and the holy alike humbled.

christ: The New Testament picks up the pattern Job describes, God humbling the wise and mighty, and places it at the center of the gospel. Paul writes that God has made foolish the wisdom of the world and chose what is weak to shame the strong (1 Corinthians 1:20, 27), quoting Isaiah and, a few chapters later, Job 5:13 (1 Corinthians 3:19). Mary sings that God has brought down rulers from their thrones and exalted the humble (Luke 1:52). The difference is direction. Job sees only the bringing down; the New Testament sees the lifting up as well, above all in the humbling of Christ to death and his exaltation by God (Philippians 2:8-9). Paul also says that in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3), the wisdom that verse 13 says belongs to God. These are thematic links, not predictions in Job's text.

hard.q: Does God deceive people? Job says the deceived and the deceiver are his.
hard.a: Verse 16 says, “True wisdom and power belong to Him. The deceived and the deceiver are His.” The line does not say that God lies. In context it means that both the one led astray and the one who leads astray remain under God's rule; neither escapes his authority. The Old Testament elsewhere speaks of God handing leaders over to confusion as judgment (Isaiah 19:14; 1 Kings 22:19-23), and interpreters differ on how to hold such passages together with the confession that God is truthful and cannot lie (Numbers 23:19; Titus 1:2). Many read them as describing God permitting and using human error within his judgment, not causing deceit as its author. Others read Job's line as his bleak observation of how the world looks, true in its affirmation of God's rule but incomplete. Either way, the verse's main point is that no human scheme, true or false, stands outside God's sovereignty.

questions: Job says those at ease look down on people in trouble. When have you caught yourself explaining someone's hardship in a way that kept you comfortable?
Job appeals to animals and the earth as teachers. What has the natural world taught you about God that argument could not?
Job's hymn dwells on God bringing down the powerful. How does that picture challenge the ways we trust in expertise, leaders, or institutions?
